extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of Reformation history / readers of historical biography
extracted.subtask_description: A literary-historical essay profiling Martin Luther, John Knox, and related Reformation phenomena; discusses their character, actions, and the social/political effects of the Reformation. Not a how-to or guideline but an interpretive account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idol-breaking / bringer-back to reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Great men (like Luther) act as 'Prophet Idol-breakers' who restore men to reality, rejecting false semblances (e.g., papal pardons seen as 'a bit of rag-paper with ink').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Luther burning the Pope's bull at Wittenberg; rhetoric: insistence that 'God's-world stood not on semblances but on realities.' Anti-patterns: accepting ceremonial or institutional semblances as if they were the underlying truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to conscience and Scripture (refusal to recant)
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not act against conscience; claims or writings based on 'sound truth and the Word of God' cannot be recanted except by clear scriptural proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: Luther at the Diet of Worms — 'Confute me by proofs of Scripture, or else by plain just arguments... Here stand I; I can do no other.' Scoring note: weight is given to demonstrable grounding in conviction and willingness to defend it publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral courage and valor
rubrics_metrics.description: True greatness involves fearless defiance of entrenched powers and spiritual threats; courage is not mere ferocity but strength rooted in conscience and affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Luther's defiance at Worms; anecdotes of defying 'Devils' (throwing inkstand at apparition). Anti-pattern: confusing mere rage or cruelty (tiger-like fierceness) with noble valor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrimination between essential and non-essential (practical tolerance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A wise reformer distinguishes essential matters of truth from non-essentials, tolerating the latter (e.g., Luther allowing a preacher to wear a cassock if it helps him).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: prioritize core doctrine/justice; tolerate liturgical or non-essential differences. Examples: Luther's response to cassock complaints; moderation in handling Karlstadt, Anabaptists, and the Peasants' War.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership by discernment and steady judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A leader must discern 'where the true heart of the matter lies' and plant himself there so others may rally; steady, kingly faculty preserves movements from descending into violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: Luther's ability to keep the Reformation relatively peaceable while alive; his 'force of silence' and moderation. Anti-pattern: revolutionary leaders who perish swept away by the movements they stir up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary strength and idiomatic expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective communicators/reformers display robust, idiomatic prose—simplicity, homeliness, rugged honesty—that can influence language and public thought (Luther's dialect became a standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Luther's 'Four-and-twenty Quartos' and the Table-Talk; guidance for evaluating writing: prize clarity, idiomatic force, and ability to 'dash out illumination.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced humanity: tenderness alongside defiance
rubrics_metrics.description: Great men combine defiance and fearlessness with tenderness, pity, and affectionate feeling—e.g., Luther's gentle behavior at his daughter's death and love of music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators: moments of grief, playful drollery, musical expression amid stern public acts. Anti-pattern: viewing sternness alone as the whole of greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformation as truth-driven action, not responsible for all consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of protesting false institutional claims is justified on truth grounds; subsequent wars and disorder are results of the falsehoods being purged, not blameable on the reformers themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: reformers' duty to answer falsehoods even if social upheaval follows (analogy to Hercules cleaning Augeas's stables). Evaluate motives and foundational aims, not only downstream effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity as the defining trait of a hero (Knox)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity—adhesion to truth regardless of consequence—is the primary heroic quality; the truthful instinct makes a man prophetic and heroic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual basis: Knox 'the truest of men' who clung to reality; anecdote: refusing to worship an image in the galleys. Scoring: prioritize consistency and authenticity of conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intolerance of falsehoods and active resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Where truth is at stake, one must actively resist and denounce falsehoods rather than blandly tolerate them; Knox's unwillingness to worship 'a painted board' exemplifies this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: Knox throwing the image into the river; his rebukes to Queen Mary. Anti-pattern: equating tolerance with passivity in the face of systemic falsehoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty-driven public speech and mobilization
rubrics_metrics.description: A potential leader has an obligation to speak and act when called by circumstance or conscience, even when personally reluctant (Knox compelled to preach despite tears).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: value the sense of duty and readiness to accept public burden; evaluate readiness to lead when community summons one, not merely ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical, cautious, patient stewardship and organizational reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective reformers combine zeal with practical caution, patience, shrewd observation and administrative ability to shape institutions (e.g., Puritanism's institutional fruits, Knox's role in Scottish Reformation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: establishment of Presbyterian structures, Puritan colonization (Mayflower) leading to durable national institutions. Anti-pattern: reckless demagogy masquerading as reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nation-building through faith-driven communal action
rubrics_metrics.description: Movements rooted in heartfelt faith can produce durable communal and national transformation (Puritanism producing civic, industrial, and intellectual fruits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mayflower settlement as the social-poetic start of America; Scottish Reformation leading to later cultural and institutional achievements (Watt, Hume, Burns). Evaluate long-term social effects, not only immediate piety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to impose moral standards on public life (theocratic impulse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some reformers (Knox) sought a public order in which religious law would guide rulers—advocating moral supremacy of Gospel over civil authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: described as Knox's 'offence'—seeking a theocracy. Guidance: when assessing such positions, note tension between moral aims and political liberty; consider implications for governance.
